summary:
Región de Los Ríos stands under Chile's national framework, and no division-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding appears in Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026. What a trans visitor faces in this region is therefore what Chilean law provides nationwide: legal gender recognition on a self-determination basis since 2019 with no medical or surgical condition attached, same-sex marriage and joint adoption since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, a third sex option on birth certificates since 2006, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, rules on entry examinations and access for trans visitors, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitoring implementation.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Institutional hostility is visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent and was denied support.

The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers, and records that the Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill in the 2025-26 rollback, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children.

Recorded abuse in Los Ríos is rising rather than falling. Movilh places the region at 1.04% of nationally documented abuse cases in 2025, a year-on-year increase of 14.28%. Nationally the report counts a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, up 27.1% and the highest total in 24 years; only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell, while the other 14 regions rose.
tangentialFactors:
Movilh reads the 2025 distribution as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate around LGBTIQ+ rights, a reading that underpins the mid-share assessment applied to Los Ríos and that cuts against treating a modest regional share as a sign of safety.

The two regions that recorded a fall in 2025 are Chile's largest metropolitan areas, where public debate is most established. Every other region, Los Ríos included, moved in the opposite direction, so the regional trajectory follows the wider national pattern rather than diverging from it.

The rollback is legislative and budgetary rather than statutory. Gender Identity Law 21.120, the 2022 marriage equality provisions and the 2012 hate-crime aggravation remain in force; what has changed is the failure of new equality and trans-rights bills, the rejection of non-discrimination reform, and the removal of the PAIG support programme from the 2026 budget bill.
localsOnly:
Residents of Región de Los Ríos change their legal gender marker through the self-determination procedure established by Gender Identity Law 21.120, in force since 2019, with no diagnosis, surgery or court hearing required. Birth certificates have offered a third sex option since 2006, and marriage and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since March 2022.

For residents, the practical loss in the current period is access to state support: the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) was excluded from the 2026 budget bill, and the decision was condemned by civil society organisations and the national ombuds for children.

Residents who report abuse appear in Movilh's national documentation at a share of 1.04% for 2025, with reported cases in the region up 14.28% year-on-year. Hate-motivated offences motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity attract aggravated penalties under the criminal code as amended in 2012.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither source supplies a Los Ríos-specific incident, arrest, prosecution, facility or detention finding. The regional figure is a percentage of a national case table, and no division-level breakdown of offence type, setting or outcome is published in the material reviewed.

The 2024 regional share is not reproduced in the 2025 edition of the Movilh report, so the year-on-year movement for Los Ríos rests on the 2025 table alone and cannot be checked against a prior-year regional figure in the same publication.

Whether the Gendarmería protocol on gender-identical housing and entry examinations is implemented in practice within this region is not sourced here; the protocol's existence is documented nationally, its regional application is unresolved. The same applies to availability of the third sex marker and of PAIG-related services at local registry and health offices after the 2026 budget exclusion.
